children: By Gregor Stuart Hunter
The dollar retreated in Asian trade on Tuesday after a holiday in some US markets, while bond yields and oil prices eased, accompanied by a slide in global stocks.
The US dollar index
of the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, slid 0.2% to 102.39, stumbling as it approached its highest since April last year.
"There are some signs that positive global economic surprises are coming off the boil, while US bond yields are stabilising," MUFG analysts wrote in a note.
The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond (US10YT=TWEB) was down 5 basis points at 5.192% as trading resumed after Monday's bond market holiday.
Brent crude futures
fell 1.4% to $105.20 as traders weighed the prospect of more diesel supplies from Russia, amid an elusive "energy truce" between Moscow and Kyiv declared by US President Donald Trump.
However, the step has brought little respite from attacks on energy infrastructure in Ukraine. Supply risks also kept in focus in the Middle East after recent attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The reversal in energy costs and climbing US Treasury bond yields undermined some of the dollar's recent strength against major peers, with no sign of a safe-haven dash for the greenback as equity markets sold off.
The euro
appreciated 0.2% to $1.1177 on Tuesday, while the British pound
The yen

strengthened 0.2% to 158.215 yen against the dollar after Bank of Japan data showed wholesale prices rose 6.8% in the year to September, missing a median market forecast of 7.6% but still enough to justify market fears of higher interest rates.
The Chinese yuan
traded near its strongest in four years, holding steady against the dollar at 6.6961 yuan in offshore trade.
The Australian dollar
was level at $0.6960, little changed after the release of minutes from the Reserve Bank of Australia's September board meeting that voted unanimously to raise rates for the fourth time this year.
The central bank said it still sees risks that inflation could prove more stubborn than assumed, leaving the door open for a fifth hike this year if needed.

"The minutes ... confirmed that the decision ... was underpinned by the Board’s view that some of the upside risks to inflation it had previously identified were materialising," Capital Economics analysts wrote in a note.
The New Zealand dollar
was up 0.1% at $0.5589, pulling away from an 18-month low.
Market attention now turns to Wednesday's US CPI report, which analysts expect to reinforce expectations for further monetary tightening.
Traders expect the Federal Reserve to sit on its hands at its next two-day meeting later this month.
Fed funds futures are pricing an implied 80.6% probability that the US central bank will remain on hold, down from 82.3% on Friday, the CME Group's FedWatch tool showed.
"Several Fed officials have pushed back against a back-to-back hike at the October 28 FOMC meeting, potentially limiting the USD’s upside," DBS analysts wrote in a note.
"Stubborn inflation also carries political costs for Republicans by reinforcing voters’ frustration with the cost of ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections."
